Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Power Generation, Inc. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Power Generation's Q3 2024 Earnings Call. Joining me on the call today are Mark Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; John Ramirez, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer, and David Patel, Chief Strategy Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that statements made during this call that are not historical facts are forward-looking statements and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. Please refer to our SEC filings for a detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Mark Reynolds.

Mark Reynolds: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on our performance this quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities, delivering solid results in a challenging environment.

Our performance was driven by:
    1.  Constructive updates on regulatory rate case filings and outcomes.
    2.  Robust storm response and recovery efforts.
    3.  Strong earnings per share performance.
    4.  Favorable comparisons to prior periods and reaffirmed guidance.
    5.  Meaningful progress toward clean energy goals and emission reductions.

Let me provide some more detail on these five key aspects before handing over to John for a deeper financial dive.

On regulatory rate cases, we've seen positive resolutions that support our investments, with strong recoveries in key states like Georgia and Florida, and promising pending dockets in North Carolina and Texas.

Storm response showcased our preparedness, with rapid restoration and lessons informing future resilience.

EPS came in strong, reflecting demand growth and cost discipline.

Versus priors, we beat expectations across the board, with raised guidance.

And on clean energy, we're accelerating renewables and cutting emissions ahead of targets.

Now, I'll turn the call over to John Ramirez to discuss the financials in detail, including these elements.

John Ramirez: Thank you, Mark. Good morning, everyone. For the Q3, we reported earnings per share of $1.42 and revenue of $2.85 billion. Our financial performance reflects the strength of our diversified business model and our disciplined approach to capital allocation.

Our capital expenditure for the quarter was $1.2 billion, primarily focused on renewables integration and grid hardening. We remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning value to shareholders. We anticipate reaffirming our full-year guidance of $5.40 to $5.60 adjusted EPS.

Let me expand on some of these drivers, starting with a comprehensive update on our regulatory rate case filings and outcomes, as these continue to be a cornerstone of our ability to recover investments in grid reliability, clean energy transition, and customer affordability. As you know, in our regulated utility business—which accounts for about 85% of our consolidated EBITDA—we operate across six states in the Southeast and Midwest, including key jurisdictions like the Georgia PSC, Florida PSC, and North Carolina UC. Our rate cases are critical for aligning authorized revenues with our escalating CapEx program, now projected at $4.8 billion for 2024, up 12% year-over-year, driven by wildfire hardening, renewables integration, and advanced grid tech.

Starting with recent outcomes: Our Georgia integrated resource and distribution rate case filed last fall with the Georgia PSC requested a $650 million revenue increase on a $12.5 billion rate base, seeking a 10.4% ROE to reflect our constructive cost of equity amid elevated 10-year Treasury yields around 4.3%. In late June, the PSC issued a final order authorizing $582 million—or 89.5% of our ask—with a forward-looking ROE of 10.25%, slightly ahead of our modeling at the midpoint of analyst expectations. This includes full recovery of our $1.2 billion AFUDC-eligible investments in the past two years, including the 450 MW solar-plus-storage hybrid project at our Albany site, now online and delivering 25% better capacity factors than standalone PV due to our 200 MWh lithium-iron-phosphate battery dispatch optimization.

Key drivers were our robust evidentiary package, including third-party cost of capital studies from experts like Regulatory Research Associates, and testimony highlighting our industry-leading SAIDI and SAIFI reliability metrics—down 15% and 18% respectively over the last three years thanks to our $300 million grid hardening initiative post-Hurricane Ida analogs. The order also incorporates a multi-year rate plan through 2026, with formula rate true-ups annually, providing revenue stability amid volatile natural gas prices, which spiked 22% in Q3 on LNG export demand.

In Florida, our May settlement in the ongoing distribution case yielded $420 million authorized on a $9.8 billion rate base, with ROE at 10.3%. This fully funds our $750 million EV infrastructure rollout, including 5,000 Level 2 chargers and 200 DC fast chargers by 2025, positioned to capture the state's 30% EV adoption growth forecast by FDOT. Notably, the PSC adopted our proposed decoupling mechanism, shielding us from weather-normalized sales declines projected at 1.2% CAGR through 2027 due to efficiency programs like our LED streetlight conversions, now at 65% penetration.

Shifting to pending filings: Our North Carolina rate case filed in March with the NCUC is on track for a Q4 decision. We're seeking $1.1 billion across transmission and distribution, on a $15.2 billion rate base growing 8% annually, with a 10.5% ROE target to match our beta of 0.85 and equity ratio of 53%. This justifies $2.3 billion in CapEx over the next three years, headlined by our 800 MW offshore wind transmission interconnect—mirroring Dominion Energy's Coastal Virginia efforts—and $400 million in DERMS to handle the influx of 1.2 GW rooftop solar from Duke Energy territory spillovers. Early procedural conferences suggest a collaborative path, with intervenors like NCSEA supporting our IRP alignment, though we're monitoring for potential ROE haircuts given the commission's recent 9.9% precedent in a Duke case.

In Texas, our ERCOT-focused generation subsidiary filed a $550 million formula rate update with the PUCT in July, emphasizing fuel cost recovery amid summer heat domes that pushed system lambdas to $5,500/MWh peaks. Pending outcome expected Q1 2025, this would recover O&M escalations of 11% tied to our gas turbine fleet overhauls—GE 7HA units now at 99.8% availability—and battery storage pilots aggregating 300 MW to arbitrage ERCOT's ancillary services market, where scarcity pricing contributed $120 million to our Q3 margins.

Broadly, we're seeing constructive trends across our footprints. Southeast commissions remain favorable, with average authorized ROEs at 10.2% versus the national utility median of 9.8% per S&P Global data, buoyed by post-storm resilience needs. Contrast this with California, where PG&E and SCE peers faced 9.5% ROEs amid wildfire claims; we're glad to avoid that exposure through our Florida and Georgia focus. Nationally, rate case lag is compressing to 10 months from 14, per EEI filings, aiding EPS delivery.

Interest rate sensitivity is a watch item: a 100 bps Fed hike could pressure our cost of capital by 75 bps on ROE, but our 70/30 debt-equity mix and fixed-rate refinancing—locking in 4.8% on $3 billion last quarter—mitigates this.

These outcomes underscore our disciplined approach: 92% recovery of filed amounts YTD, funding a CapEx-to-Opex ratio of 2.8x, well above peers. Strategically, we're leveraging rate cases to accelerate our net-zero pathway—30% renewables by 2027, including Form Energy iron-air storage pilots for 100-hour dispatch—and resilience against EIA-projected 15% demand growth from data centers in the Southeast. Customer bills rise modestly at 4.2% annualized, below inflation, thanks to our decoupled rate designs and virtual power plant aggregations with Enel X.

Looking forward, we expect $2.5 billion in new rate authorizations by year-end, supporting 6-8% EPS growth. Our IRP filings in all states align with IRA incentives, positioning us to capture $500 million in PTC/ITC extensions for our 1.5 GW pipeline.

Now, turning to EPS performance and drivers: We delivered adjusted EPS of $1.42 for the quarter, up 22% year-over-year from $1.16 in Q3 2023, and ahead of consensus expectations by $0.08. On a GAAP basis, EPS was $1.32, reflecting some one-time integration costs from our recent acquisition of the 1,200 MW Mystic CT assets in ISO-NE.

Consolidated revenues reached $2.85 billion, a 12% increase YoY, fueled primarily by our regulated electric segment, which grew to $2.1 billion. Retail sales volumes were up on a weather-normalized basis, with load growth reflecting hyperscale data center demand—particularly in our PJM and MISO footprints, where hyperscalers like Amazon Web Services and Microsoft have contracted over 1.5 GW of firm capacity. Industrial loads contributed further uplift, driven by manufacturing reshoring in the Midwest.

Transmission and distribution revenues benefited from higher ROE-authorized returns under ongoing rate cases. On the competitive side, our merchant gas fleet dispatched at high capacity factors, capturing elevated spark spreads amid summer heat waves, with average realized power prices well above priors. Natural gas hedging played a pivotal role: much of our needs are locked in below the forward curve.

Operating expenses were controlled despite pressures. O&M benefited from our predictive maintenance program using digital twin technology across CCGT units, reducing forced outage rates and avoiding lost opportunities. Fuel costs were managed through our diversified portfolio—gas, nuclear, renewables, coal—with nuclear achieving top-tier capacity factors.

Depreciation rose with capex, primarily for BESS and solar augmentation qualifying for IRA benefits. Interest expense stable post green bond issuance.

Our effective tax rate benefited from PTC/ITC from wind portfolio performance. Shares outstanding reduced via repurchases.

Regionally, Northeast PJM pricing drove merchant margins; Midwest transmission offset weather; Texas reliability premiums boosted EBITDA; West renewables secured PPAs.

Strategically, results support our clean capacity growth: retiring uneconomic coal, repowering with hybrids, partnerships for offshore wind, AI load forecasting, data center wheeling.

For comparisons to prior periods and updated guidance: Revenues up 12% YoY from $2.54 billion in Q3 2023 and 8% sequentially from Q2 2024's $2.64 billion. Adjusted EBITDA at $825 million, up 18% YoY from $700 million and 11% from Q2's $745 million. Diluted EPS up 22% YoY; net income $380 million versus $310 million.

Tailwinds: Data center demand up 15% YoY, favorable ISO/RTO prices, hedging, hotter CDDs driving 10% load uplift.

Segment-wise: Regulated utilities EBITDA $450 million, up 14% YoY, rate base $28 billion up 7%, ROE 11.2%; Competitive generation $310 million up 25% YoY, fleet capacity factor 72%; Renewables $65 million doubled YoY.

Free cash flow $550 million up 20% YoY, supporting dividends and buybacks; leverage 3.1x.

Generation 28.5 TWh up 9% YoY; fuel costs benign.

Regionally strong in PJM, ERCOT; accelerating decarbonization with capex skewed to renewables, nuclear extensions, CCUS.

Raising FY2024 guidance: Adjusted EBITDA $3.15-$3.25 billion, EPS $5.40-$5.60, capex $4.8-$5.0 billion, FCF $2.1-$2.3 billion. Initial 2025: EBITDA $3.45-$3.65 billion, EPS $5.90-$6.20.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, John. Let me provide an update on the operational front. We are seeing improved efficiency in our gas-fired CCGT power plants due to the implementation of predictive maintenance digital twin technology. This has resulted in a 25 basis point reduction in forced outages.

David Patel: Thank you, Lisa. Turning to our long-term strategy, we are actively exploring opportunities in the battery storage and small modular reactor space. We believe this will be a key driver of future growth.

Before questions, let me touch deeper on our progress toward clean energy goals and emission reductions. Apex has committed to net-zero Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by 2045—five years ahead of many peers—and 80% emissions intensity reduction from a 2005 baseline by 2030. This drives rate base growth, IRA incentives, and premium PPAs with hyperscalers.

In the first nine months of 2024, adjusted Scope 1 and 2 emissions totaled 12.4 million metric tons CO2e—a 22% YoY reduction and 48% below 2005 baseline. Intensity at 312 g CO2e/MWh, down 28% YoY, beating S&P Utilities average. Scope 3 down 15%; NOx 14,500 tons down 18%; SO2 negligible.

Renewables capacity 18.7 GW, up 32% YoY, 52% of total 36 GW portfolio—ahead of targets. Q3 commissions: 500 MW Southeast solar (bifacial PERC 22.5% efficiency), 250 MW Texas wind (48% capacity factors), 100 MW/400 MWh BESS.

Generation: Renewables 41% of 58 TWh YTD, up from 29%; gas 45% down from 52%; coal 9% down 15%.

Southeast: 60% carbon-free, 1.2 GW solar pipeline with IRA ITC; emissions down 25%. ERCOT/CAISO: 1.5 GW BESS queue, $45M ancillary revenue; sub-200 g/MWh. International: 2 GW offshore wind 15% output growth.

R&D: Green H2 blending, DAC for 45Q, NuScale SMR MOU.

Accretive: $2.8B renewables capex 8-10% returns, 70% fixed PPAs, $450M IRA funding, rate base $42B up 12%.

2025: 25% emissions cut, 5 GW adds, net-zero Scope 1 gas.

Mark Reynolds: Thank you, John, Lisa, and David. Now, we'll open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Sarah Jenkins with Morningstar. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins: Thanks, and good morning team. Could you walk us through the storm response and recovery efforts in more detail, particularly the financial implications and any lessons learned for future resiliency?

John Ramirez: Good morning, Sarah. Happy to dive into this. I'll turn it over to our COO Lisa Chen, who's been leading our storm initiatives firsthand. Lisa?

Lisa Chen: Thanks, John, and good morning, Sarah. Absolutely, storm response and recovery remains a critical focus for Apex Power Generation, especially as we're seeing these events intensify across our five-state footprint—Florida, Georgia, the Carolinas, Texas, and the Midwest. Let me break this down systematically: the event overview, our response metrics, cost dynamics, regional nuances, technical advancements, and strategic forward path.

First, context on the event. We're recapping our response to Hurricane Zeta in late October, which made landfall as a Category 2 near Tampa Bay, followed by a polar vortex event in mid-February across our Texas and Midwest territories. Combined, these storms caused peak outages for 1.25 million customers—about 18% of our total 7 million served—peaking at 825,000 metered customers down simultaneously. That's comparable to the 1.1 million peak from Hurricane Ida in '21 but with 15% higher wind gusts in Florida per NOAA data.

On response: We mobilized within T+2 hours of the NWS watch, activating our Emergency Operations Center in Atlanta and invoking mutual assistance pacts through the Edison Electric Institute's SER program. We brought in over 12,000 external resources—5,200 lineworkers, 2,100 tree crews, and 4,700 support personnel—from partners like Duke Energy, Southern Company, and Oncor in Texas. This was our largest deployment since Winter Storm Uri in '21, where we coordinated 10,000 resources.

Restoration metrics were strong: We achieved 95% restoration within 48 hours for Zeta—beating our internal target of 72 hours—and full SAIDI normalization to pre-storm levels by Day 5, with a storm-related SAIDI of 1,200 minutes versus the industry benchmark of 1,500 from IEEE Gold Book data. SAIFI came in at 2.8 interruptions per customer, a 12% improvement YoY, thanks to pre-positioned assets. In Texas, the vortex event saw us restore 85% of impacted customers in under 24 hours, mitigating ERCOT's broader grid stress.

Financially, total storm costs hit $285 million pre-tax, up 22% from our $235 million in '23 storm O&M due to higher vegetation management and contractor rates amid labor inflation. Breakdown: $140 million O&M (pole replacements, wire stringing), $95 million CapEx (primarily underground conversions and substation hardening), and $50 million in customer credits under our Florida PSC-mandated goodwill program. Positively, insurance recoveries are tracking at $165 million, or 58% of total costs, with the balance recoverable via regulatory mechanisms—our Storm Cost Rider in Georgia and Texas, and securitization clauses in Florida akin to FPL's post-Irma model. This flows through to Q4 adjusted EPS dilution of just $0.08, well within our guidance buffer, and we expect full recovery in '25 rates.

Regionally, Florida bore 60% of the load—our Tampa and Jacksonville divisions saw 750,000 outages from 130 mph gusts, snapping 4,200 poles and requiring 1,200 miles of reconductoring. Texas was next at 25%, with ice accretion up to 2 inches causing 18kV feeder failures in DFW; our microgrid pilots at two Houston industrial sites kept 15 MW islanded seamlessly. The Carolinas and Midwest were lighter at 15% combined, but winter storm hardening from '22 investments paid off—zero major transformer failures.

Technically, we leaned into our $150 million digital resiliency suite rolled out post-Ida. Drones with LiDAR surveyed 40% of damaged corridors, cutting pole inspection times by 35% versus manual crews; our Outage Management System (OMS), integrated with Esri GIS and IBM Maximo, used AI-driven predictive analytics to prioritize 80kV feeders, reducing CAIDI by 18% to 430 minutes. We also piloted GE Grid Solutions' synchrophasors for real-time grid stability during ERCOT frequency dips, preventing cascading outages. Vegetation management via LiDAR-enabled growth modeling trimmed trim cycles by 20%, addressing NERC VEG-001 compliance proactively.

Strategically, these events underscore our $2.2 billion five-year Grid Hardening Plan, approved by FERC and state commissions last quarter. Key pillars: 30% undergrounding of coastal 12kV laterals by '27 (1,500 miles already done), 500 MW of BESS for auto-reclose resiliency—like our 100 MW Fluence pilot in Savannah—and advanced AMI upgrades to 98% penetration for faster outage detection. We're targeting a 25% SAIDI reduction long-term, aligning with NARUC resiliency goals amid climate trends: EIA data shows U.S. major outage events up 30% since 2010, with costs averaging $50B annually industry-wide.

Lessons learned? Dual-storm sequencing strains supply chains—pole lead times stretched to 10 days—so we're stockpiling 20k Class 1 poles via partnerships with Koppers. Also, accelerating DER integration: Post-Zeta, we fast-tracked 50 MW of customer-sited solar-plus-storage under our Texas ConnectDER program, reducing restoration dependency.

Overall, while storms pressure near-term margins—O&M up 8% YoY excluding weather—we're turning adversity into regulated revenue streams, with $400 million in rate base growth from recovery CapEx. John, back to you for any financial tie-ins.

John Ramirez: Perfect, Lisa—spot on. Sarah, this reinforces our '25 guidance of $4.20-$4.40 EPS in normalized scenarios, with storm normalization baked in. We're positioned resiliently as peers like NextEra and Dominion face similar headwinds.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mike Harlan with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Mike Harlan: Good morning. Can you elaborate on your plans for data center load growth and interconnection queue management?

Mark Reynolds: Certainly, Mike. We're capitalizing on the hyperscaler boom with over 800 MW of wheeling agreements YTD, targeting 5-7% annual load growth through 2030. Our 5 GW queue benefits from FERC Order 2023 fast-tracking, with AI-optimized forecasting via Siemens software to prioritize. We've got firm contracts with AWS and Microsoft, aligning with our clean capacity framework.

Operator: Our next question comes from Emily Ross with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Emily Ross: What is your outlook for regulatory risks and interest rate impacts?

John Ramirez: Great question, Emily. With 92% recovery YTD in rate cases and compressing lags, we're well-positioned. On rates, our fixed-rate debt at 4.8% and 70/30 mix buffers 100 bps hikes to just 75 bps ROE pressure. Constructive Southeast trends versus national medians support 6-8% EPS growth.

Operator: Our next question comes from Tom Whitaker with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Tom Whitaker: How are you mitigating risks related to supply chain delays in renewables?

Lisa Chen: Tom, good morning. Supply chain headwinds like Nextracker delays affected two projects, but our 85% domestic content for ITC bonuses and partnerships with First Solar/Vestas keep us on track for 5 GW 2025 adds. Stockpiling trackers and HVDC via diversified suppliers, plus R&D in alternatives like monopiles for offshore.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the call back over to Mark Reynolds for closing remarks.

Mark Reynolds: Thank you. In summary, we delivered solid results in the Q3, demonstrating the strength of our business model and our commitment to creating long-term value for our shareholders. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and positioning Apex Power Generation for continued success. Thank you for your time and interest in Apex Power Generation.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
